tagline: Pine tar for wooden ships gave North Carolinians a lasting nickname
intro: Tar Heel Trace belongs to North Carolina’s Coastal Plain scenic-byway collection. NCDOT selects these routes to present the state’s history, geography and culture. Wilson grew with the railroad; Williamston stands beside the Roanoke River.

The Tar Heel nickname grew from North Carolina’s production of tar, pitch and turpentine from pine trees. Workers burned piled pine logs to release oil; tar and pitch sealed wooden ship hulls and protected them from shipworms.
Begin in Wilson, whose downtown station dates to 1924. Conetoe takes its name from nearby Conetoe Creek. Finish in Williamston, where the Roanoke River forms the town’s northern boundary.

moments.title: Wilson
moments.text: The railroad helped turn the community of Toisnot into the city now called Wilson. The Wilmington and Raleigh Railroad Company began its Wilmington-to-Weldon line in 1836 and reached the community in 1839. North-south service followed by 1840, stimulating growth. The downtown station belongs to a later railway era: the Atlantic Coast Line built it in 1924. The city purchased the station and its separate express building in 1994, then restored them between 1996 and 1998. Renamed for G. K. Butterfield in 2024, the station is part of the city’s Central Business–Tobacco Warehouse Historic District.

moments.title: Conetoe
moments.text: Conetoe began in 1887 under a different name, Warren Station. The name changed to match nearby Conetoe Creek. Pronounced kuh-NEE-tuh, the town is in Edgecombe County.

moments.title: Williamston
moments.text: Williamston’s northern edge meets the Roanoke River, which also marks the Bertie County line. Founded in 1779, the town was named for William Williams, a local military commander during the American Revolution. Its commercial historic district gathers buildings from the mid-nineteenth century through the 1920s. Greek Revival, Colonial Revival and Romanesque buildings are among the styles represented in the commercial district. The district also includes the 1938 post office, whose mural depicts the Wright brothers’ first flight at Kitty Hawk. Philip von Saltza painted it in 1940 as part of a federal mural project.
